verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–18 — The Man Who Has Seen Affliction
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One man now speaks, and he speaks of God as his attacker. I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath (v. 1). He has been driven into darkness (v. 2), his body broken (v. 4), walled in and chained (v. 7), his prayer shut out (v. 8). God has been a bear and a lion to him (v. 10), an archer with him as the target (vv. 12-13), and his own people laugh at him (v. 14). He has eaten gravel and forgotten what happiness is (vv. 16-17), until he says the bleakest thing he has said: My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD (v. 18).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer may reach the point of saying his hope is gone — and still be saying it to the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath; he has driven and brought me into darkness without any light; surely against me he turns his hand again and again the whole day long.
verseByVerse.commentary:
I am the man who has seen affliction under the rod of his wrath;

The first two poems spoke about a city. Now a single man steps forward, and the whole book narrows to one person's suffering. He does not give his name. His experience is so close to Jeremiah's — mocked by his own people, thrown into a pit — that many have heard the prophet's voice here. But he speaks as someone who carries the nation's grief in his own body, so that anyone who has suffered can stand where he stands.

I am the man who has seen affliction. He has not heard about it or read about it. He has seen it, lived inside it. And it came under the rod of his wrath. He does not even need to say whose. Everyone knows.

he has driven and brought me into darkness without any light;

Darkness is bad enough. Without any light is worse — not a dim room but no lamp at all, no sense of direction, no way to see where the next step goes. Many believers know this: a season where God seems completely absent and nothing makes sense. The Bible does not pretend that season never comes. Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God (Isa 50:10).

surely against me he turns his hand again and again the whole day long.

One blow can be survived. What wears a person down is again and again the whole day long — the diagnosis followed by the job loss followed by the family crisis, with no gap to breathe. He feels singled out: against me.

verseByVerse.quote: He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones; he has besieged and enveloped me with bitterness and tribulation; he has made me dwell in darkness like the dead of long ago.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has made my flesh and my skin waste away; he has broken my bones;

The suffering is physical. Skin, flesh, bones — the famine and siege wrote themselves on the body. Scripture never treats the body as unimportant to God, and it never treats bodily pain as unspiritual.

And yet the God who breaks bones is the God who mends them. David, crushed by his own sin, prayed let the bones that you have broken rejoice (Ps 51:8). He did not look for healing anywhere else. The hand that broke is the hand he asked to heal.

he has besieged and enveloped me with bitterness and tribulation;

This is what had happened to Jerusalem: an army built siege works around it until no one could get in or out. Now he says God has done that to him personally — surrounded him with bitterness and tribulation, so that every direction he turns he meets it.

he has made me dwell in darkness like the dead of long ago.

Not just dying but like the dead of long ago — the long-forgotten dead, whom no one visits. A psalmist said the same: You have put me in the depths of the pit, in the regions dark and deep (Ps 88:6). That psalm ends in darkness too. God has put such prayers in his book so that no sufferer will ever think his darkness is too dark to bring to God.

verseByVerse.quote: He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy; though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer; he has blocked my ways with blocks of stones; he has made my paths crooked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has walled me about so that I cannot escape; he has made my chains heavy;

Walls and chains: a prisoner with no way out. Job used the same picture — He has walled up my way, so that I cannot pass (Job 19:8). Every exit he tries is blocked.

though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer;

This is the cruellest line so far. He is not only suffering; he is praying, loudly — I call and cry for help — and it feels as if the prayers hit the ceiling. God shuts out his prayer as someone shuts a door.

Christians sometimes say that God always answers prayer. That is true, but it is not how it always feels, and this verse gives permission to say so. Hold on to this line, though, because at the end of this chapter the same man says you heard my plea (v. 56). The door was not locked forever. And the Son of God, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications, with loud cries and tears, and he was heard (Heb 5:7) — so that through him no believer's prayer is ever truly shut out.

he has blocked my ways with blocks of stones; he has made my paths crooked.

Every road he takes ends in a wall, and every path twists back on itself. Plans fail. Nothing goes straight. That is exactly how life feels under God's discipline.

verseByVerse.quote: He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding; he turned aside my steps and tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate; he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow. He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver;
verseByVerse.commentary:
He is a bear lying in wait for me, a lion in hiding; he turned aside my steps and tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate;

Now the pictures become violent. God is a bear waiting in ambush, a lion crouched in the undergrowth. The man walks into the trap and is torn to pieces.

How can a believer speak of God like this? Because it is honest about how affliction feels, and because the Bible itself uses these images for God's judgment (Hos 5:14). The man is not saying God is cruel. He is saying God is not safe to trifle with — which is exactly what Judah forgot.

Look again at the words tore me to pieces; he has made me desolate. Hosea used that same picture and drew from it a surprising conclusion: Come, let us return to the LORD; for he has torn us, that he may heal us; he has struck us down, and he will bind us up (Hos 6:1). A lion tears to kill. God tears to heal. The wound is real, but its purpose is not destruction; it is return.

he bent his bow and set me as a target for his arrow.

He drove into my kidneys the arrows of his quiver;

He feels like the target on an archery range, and every arrow finds its mark, driven deep into the body. Job described the same experience: he set me up as his target; his archers surround me (Job 16:12-13).

There is comfort even in the fact that these words exist. You are not the first believer to feel that God has made you his target. Job felt it. This man felt it. And the Son of God, who truly stood under the arrows of God's wrath at the cross, felt it most of all — not for his sins but for ours.

verseByVerse.quote: I have become the laughingstock of all my people, the object of their taunts all day long. He has filled me with bitterness; he has sated me with wormwood. He has made my teeth grind on gravel, and made me cower in ashes;
verseByVerse.commentary:
I have become the laughingstock of all my people, the object of their taunts all day long.

The ESV notes that some manuscripts read "all peoples." Either way, the mockery is public and constant. But if it is my people, the wound is deeper: those who should have stood with him laugh at him.

Jeremiah knew exactly this: I have become a laughingstock all the day; everyone mocks me (Jer 20:7). So did Jesus, mocked by the soldiers who knelt before him and cried Hail, King of the Jews! (Matt 27:29).

He has filled me with bitterness; he has sated me with wormwood.

Wormwood was a plant with an intensely bitter taste, and it became a byword for bitterness in life. To be sated with it is to have eaten nothing else, to have bitterness as your whole diet.

He has made my teeth grind on gravel, and made me cower in ashes;

Imagine biting into bread and finding it full of grit. That is the picture — every mouthful hurts. And he is made to cower in ashes, pressed down into the ruin of his burned city. Humiliation and pain together.

verseByVerse.quote: my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is; so I say, "My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
my soul is bereft of peace; I have forgotten what happiness is;

Bereft of peace — peace has been taken from him like a family member taken by death. And I have forgotten what happiness is. The ESV notes that the Hebrew word behind happiness is "good." He has forgotten what good is. He cannot even remember what it felt like.

Keep that note in mind. In a few verses the same man will say good three times over (vv. 25-27). He does not remember the good by looking at his circumstances. He relearns it by looking at God.

so I say, "My endurance has perished; so has my hope from the LORD."

This is the bottom of the pit. My endurance has perished — I cannot keep going. So has my hope from the LORD — I no longer expect anything from God.

Scripture lets a believer say that. Elijah said something like it under the broom tree: It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life (1 Kgs 19:4).

But notice something. Even at the bottom, he names the LORD. He says his hope from the LORD has perished — and in saying it, he is still talking about the LORD, still defining his hope by him. A person who has truly let go of God does not grieve the loss of hope in God. The very ache of this verse is a sign that faith is not dead, only exhausted. And the next verses show what exhausted faith does next.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — But This I Call to Mind
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man remembers his affliction, and the memory bows him down (vv. 19-20). Then he chooses to remember something else: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope (v. 21). The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness (vv. 22-23). Everything else has been taken, and he finds what is left: The LORD is my portion, says my soul, therefore I will hope in him (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Hope in the ruins does not come from the circumstances but from calling to mind the unchanging character of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall! My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Remember my affliction and my wanderings, the wormwood and the gall!

He calls on God to remember — the same prayer the whole book prays. My wanderings is the homelessness of exile. The wormwood and the gall are the bitterness again: gall was a byword for poison.

When Jesus hung on the cross, they offered him wine to drink, mixed with gall, and he would not drink it (Matt 27:34). He refused it. He had come to drink another cup — the bitterness of God's wrath — to the bottom.

My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down within me.

Here is the problem with memory. He cannot stop thinking about it, and the more he thinks, the lower he sinks. That is what rumination does: turning the same pain over and over until the soul is bent double.

Many people live exactly here. They replay the betrayal, the diagnosis, the mistake, the loss, night after night. The next verse does not tell him to stop remembering. It tells him what else to remember.

verseByVerse.quote: But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope:

This is the hinge of the whole book. But.

Nothing outside has changed. The city is still in ruins. His body is still broken. The enemies are still laughing. What has changed is what he is deliberately bringing to mind. This I call to mind — he makes himself remember, the way you might take hold of a railing in the dark.

That is how hope works in Scripture. It is not a mood that comes over you. It is the result of preaching truth to yourself. David did it when his men wanted to stone him: David strengthened himself in the LORD his God (1 Sam 30:6). A psalmist did it: I will remember the deeds of the LORD; yes, I will remember your wonders of old (Ps 77:11). You may not be able to feel your way out of despair. But you can call something to mind.

The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end;

Here is what he calls to mind. Not a technique, not a positive outlook, but a fact about God.

Steadfast love is God's loyal, committed love to his covenant people — the love he proclaimed to Moses when he passed by: a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness (Exod 34:6). It is love that has bound itself by promise and will not let go.

The ESV notes that the Hebrew text here reads "Because of the steadfast love of the LORD, we are not cut off," while the ESV follows the Syriac and the Targum. Both readings stand on the same truth. Either God's love never ceases, or it is the reason we have not ceased. Jerusalem had been struck to the ground — but not wiped out. There were survivors, and there was someone left alive to write this poem. That alone was proof that God's love had not run out.

And set this beside chapter 2, where the Lord swallowed up without mercy (2:2). The mercy had been withheld from the city's walls. It had not been exhausted in God's heart. His mercies never come to an end.

they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.

New every morning. Think of the manna in the wilderness: Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat (Exod 16:21). It could not be stored up. Each day needed each day's gift. God's mercies are like that. Yesterday's mercy was sufficient for yesterday. Today's mercy is waiting for today, and tomorrow's will be there tomorrow. That is why Jesus taught us to pray Give us this day our daily bread (Matt 6:11), and not to be anxious about tomorrow (Matt 6:34).

Some mornings you wake and the weight comes back before you have even opened your eyes. On those mornings, remember that there is a fresh supply of mercy which did not exist last night, and it was made for this morning.

And then he turns and speaks straight to God: great is your faithfulness. Not "great was your faithfulness" in the good old days. Great is — now, here, among the ashes. God's faithfulness is not measured by our circumstances but by his promises, and he keeps them. If we are faithless, he remains faithful — for he cannot deny himself (2 Tim 2:13).

verseByVerse.quote: "The LORD is my portion," says my soul, "therefore I will hope in him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD is my portion," says my soul, "therefore I will hope in him."

A portion was a share of the inheritance, a piece of land to live on and farm. When Israel entered Canaan, every tribe received a portion except one. To the priests God said: You shall have no inheritance in their land... I am your portion and your inheritance (Num 18:20).

Now every Israelite is in that position. The land is lost; chapter 5 will say Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers (5:2). The house, the fields, the temple — gone. And the man says: I still have my portion. The LORD himself.

That is where hope becomes unshakeable. If your portion is your health, your family, your reputation or your savings, it can be taken, and then your hope goes with it. If your portion is the LORD, nothing can take it. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps 73:26).

Notice who says it: says my soul. He is talking to himself again, the way verse 21 began. And the conclusion follows: therefore I will hope in him. Not "I feel hopeful" but "I will hope." Hope is a decision made on the basis of who God is.

Christians can say this with more certainty than he could, because God has given us not only himself but his Son. He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things? (Rom 8:32).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 25–39 — It Is Good to Wait Quietly
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The man who had forgotten what good is now says good three times: the LORD is good to those who wait for him, it is good to wait quietly for his salvation, it is good to bear the yoke in youth (vv. 25-27). So the sufferer sits in silence, puts his mouth in the dust and turns his cheek (vv. 28-30), for the Lord will not cast off forever and he does not afflict from his heart (vv. 31-33). The Lord does not approve of human injustice (vv. 34-36), yet nothing happens unless he has commanded it, and good and bad alike come from the mouth of the Most High; so why should a living man complain about the punishment of his sins? (vv. 37-39).
verseByVerse.theology: God is sovereign over affliction, never cruel in it, and never the approver of the injustice he overrules.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him. It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD. It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The LORD is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him.

He had forgotten what good is (v. 17). Now, in three verses in a row, the word comes back: the LORD is good, it is good to wait, it is good to bear the yoke. The good he could not find in his circumstances he has found in God.

To those who wait for him. Waiting in the Bible is not passive. It is leaning your whole weight on God while nothing seems to happen. And it is paired with the soul who seeks him — waiting is active seeking. They who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength (Isa 40:31).

It is good that one should wait quietly for the salvation of the LORD.

Quietly. Not without prayer — this book is full of loud prayer — but without the frantic, fretting, grasping panic that tries to force God's hand or find a way out apart from him. In quietness and in trust shall be your strength (Isa 30:15). Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for him (Ps 37:7).

Waiting quietly is hard for people who are used to fixing things. But some things only God can fix, and the most useful thing to do is to wait for him and keep seeking him.

It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth.

A young ox learns to pull by wearing the yoke. It chafes. But an animal that never bore a yoke is useless for the plough. Hard things learned early shape a life: Before I was afflicted I went astray, but now I keep your word (Ps 119:67).

This is a word for young people going through hard things, and for parents who long to spare their children every difficulty. Some yokes are gifts. And there is one yoke that every young person should take up as early as possible: Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29).

verseByVerse.quote: Let him sit alone in silence when it is laid on him; let him put his mouth in the dust— there may yet be hope; let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and let him be filled with insults.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let him sit alone in silence when it is laid on him;

When the yoke of affliction is laid on you, the first response is not to argue or to explain it but to sit alone in silence. There is a silence of rebellion, sulking at God. This is the other kind — the silence of someone who has recognised God's hand. I am mute; I do not open my mouth, for it is you who have done it (Ps 39:9).

let him put his mouth in the dust— there may yet be hope;

To put your mouth in the dust is to lie face down — the posture of a subject before a king. It is total humility. And notice the quiet line tucked in: there may yet be hope. Not certainty, not a guarantee of how things will turn out, but a door left open. Humility is where hope can begin, because humility stops demanding and starts trusting. Humble yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God so that at the proper time he may exalt you (1 Pet 5:6).

let him give his cheek to the one who strikes, and let him be filled with insults.

This must be read carefully. The chapter is about accepting God's discipline humbly, not about excusing human cruelty; in a few verses it will say plainly that the Lord does not approve of injustice (vv. 34-36). This verse does not tell anyone to stay in harm's way or to treat abuse as God's will. It describes a person who has stopped fighting God, and so no longer needs to hit back at those God uses to humble him.

And here the chapter points straight to Christ. The Servant of the LORD said I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard (Isa 50:6). At his trial, they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67). When he was reviled, he did not revile in return... but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Pet 2:23). The man in Lamentations gave his cheek because he had sinned. Jesus gave his because we had.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord will not cast off forever, for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love; for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
For the Lord will not cast off forever,

Now come the reasons why a sufferer can wait quietly. Three times: for. The first is that the rejection is not permanent. The Lord will not cast off forever. There is an end to discipline, even when you cannot see it. For his anger is but for a moment, and his favor is for a lifetime. Weeping may tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning (Ps 30:5).

for, though he cause grief, he will have compassion according to the abundance of his steadfast love;

The second reason: the grief is real — he cause grief — but compassion follows it, and not a small compassion. It is measured according to the abundance of his steadfast love. The grief has a limit. The love does not.

for he does not afflict from his heart or grieve the children of men.

The third reason goes deepest. God does afflict, and this book has not hidden it for a moment. But he does not afflict from his heart. It is not what he delights in. It is not the centre of who he is.

Ezekiel heard God say the same: I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live (Ezek 33:11). Isaiah called judgment God's strange deed and alien work (Isa 28:21). Mercy is his heart; judgment is the work his holiness requires when mercy is refused.

This changes how a believer can think about suffering. When God disciplines his children, he is not enjoying it. He disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness (Heb 12:10). A father who must correct his child does it with a heavy heart, and God's heart is heavier and kinder than any father's.

And the proof of what is in God's heart is the cross. There God did the one thing that did come from his heart — he gave his Son out of love — so that his wrath would be satisfied and his compassion could flow freely to sinners.

verseByVerse.quote: To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the earth, to deny a man justice in the presence of the Most High, to subvert a man in his lawsuit, the Lord does not approve.
verseByVerse.commentary:
To crush underfoot all the prisoners of the earth,

to deny a man justice in the presence of the Most High,

to subvert a man in his lawsuit, the Lord does not approve.

These three verses build to one statement, which comes at the very end: the Lord does not approve. Crushing prisoners, twisting justice in court, cheating someone in a lawsuit — God sees these things and does not approve of any of them.

Why is this here? Because a person who has just said that his suffering comes from God's hand may be tempted to think that everything done to him must therefore be right. It is not. The Babylonians who crushed Judah's prisoners were God's instrument, and they were also guilty. God's sovereignty does not make him the author of anyone's cruelty or the approver of anyone's injustice.

Joseph could say to his brothers you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good (Gen 50:20). Both halves were true. And at the cross the same double truth reached its peak: Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and his killers were still lawless men (Acts 2:23).

Note the phrase in the presence of the Most High. Every courtroom on earth sits in the presence of a higher court. Injustice that no human judge corrects is not unseen. For anyone who has been wronged and never had justice, that is solid comfort. For anyone who has done the wronging, it is a solemn warning.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it? Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come? Why should a living man complain, a man, about the punishment of his sins?
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it?

Is it not from the mouth of the Most High that good and bad come?

Now the other side of the truth. God disapproves of injustice, and yet nothing happens outside his command. Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it? Human plans, Babylon's included, come to pass only because God permits and directs them.

And good and bad alike come from the mouth of the Most High. Job said: Shall we receive good from God, and shall we not receive evil? (Job 2:10). Isaiah: I make well-being and create calamity (Isa 45:7). The Bible holds this truth without apology, because the alternative is far worse. If there is disaster God does not control, then there is disaster that has no purpose and no end.

This is not a cold doctrine. It is the only thing that makes verse 22 possible. If God controls the bad, then his steadfast love can reach into it, limit it and use it. For those who love God all things work together for good (Rom 8:28).

Why should a living man complain, a man, about the punishment of his sins?

Two things stand out. First, a living man. He is still alive. After everything, he is still breathing, which the Hebrew reading of verse 22 says is itself a mercy. The punishment has been less than the sin.

Second, complain. This book is full of lament — honest crying out to God. Complaint in this sense is different. It is the grumbling that accuses God of being unfair. Lament says, "Lord, this hurts; please look." Complaint says, "Lord, I don't deserve this." The man has already admitted that it is the punishment of his sins. So he may lament, and he must not complain.

Christians need to keep that line clear too. We may bring every tear to God. But no Christian ever receives what his sins deserve, because Christ received it. He does not deal with us according to our sins, nor repay us according to our iniquities (Ps 103:10).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–54 — Let Us Test and Examine Our Ways
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The I becomes we: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD! (v. 40). The people confess that they have transgressed and rebelled, and that God has not yet forgiven (v. 42). He has wrapped himself in anger and in a cloud that no prayer can pass (vv. 43-44); they have become scum and garbage among the nations (v. 45). The speaker weeps without ceasing until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees (v. 50), and remembers being hunted, thrown into a pit and covered by water until he said I am lost (vv. 52-54).
verseByVerse.theology: Real repentance examines its own ways, confesses without excuse, and keeps praying until God looks down.

verseByVerse.quote: Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD! Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven: "We have transgressed and rebelled, and you have not forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Let us test and examine our ways, and return to the LORD!

Suddenly I becomes us. The man who has spoken for himself now calls the whole people to do what he has done.

And what is the first thing to do in suffering? Not to examine God's ways but our ways. That is backwards from how most people react. We ask why God allowed this; Lamentations asks what we have done and where we need to turn. It is the prodigal son in the far country: when he came to himself, he said, I will arise and go to my father (Luke 15:17-18).

Examination is not an end in itself. Its purpose is to return to the LORD. Self-examination that stays turned inward becomes morbid. Self-examination that leads to God becomes repentance. Search me, O God, and know my heart!... And see if there be any grievous way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting! (Ps 139:23-24).

Let us lift up our hearts and hands to God in heaven:

Hearts and hands. Lifting hands was the posture of prayer; Judah had lifted hands plenty of times in the temple. What was missing was the heart. Rend your hearts and not your garments (Joel 2:13). God wants the inside to go up with the outside.

"We have transgressed and rebelled, and you have not forgiven.

The confession is short and complete. No excuses, no mitigating circumstances. We have transgressed and rebelled.

Then an honest, painful line: and you have not forgiven. The judgment has not been lifted. The exile goes on. They have confessed, and the consequences remain.

That is a hard reality even for Christians: confessing a sin does not always remove its consequences in this life. But the Christian can say something the exiles could not yet say, because Christ has come. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9). The consequences may linger. The guilt does not. There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:1).

verseByVerse.quote: "You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity; you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through. You have made us scum and garbage among the peoples.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us, killing without pity;

The confession turns back into lament. God has put on anger like a garment and chased them down.

you have wrapped yourself with a cloud so that no prayer can pass through.

Twice: you have wrapped yourself. First with anger, then with a cloud. The cloud that once filled the temple with glory now blocks prayer like a wall. Your iniquities have made a separation between you and your God, and your sins have hidden his face from you so that he does not hear (Isa 59:2).

Here the gospel speaks with great power. When Jesus died, the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom (Matt 27:51). The barrier between sinners and God was opened from God's side. Now Christ has entered into heaven itself, now to appear in the presence of God on our behalf (Heb 9:24), and he always lives to make intercession for those who come to God through him (Heb 7:25). For anyone in Christ, there is no cloud that prayer cannot pass through.

You have made us scum and garbage among the peoples.

The chosen people have become the rubbish of the nations — what everyone else throws away.

The apostle Paul used almost the same words for the life of an apostle: We have become, and are still, like the scum of the world, the refuse of all things (1 Cor 4:13). But for Paul it was not judgment. It was the privilege of following a Lord who was himself treated as refuse, crucified outside the city like something thrown out. What Judah suffered as the penalty of sin, Christ took on as the price of love, and his people share it as the mark of belonging to him.

verseByVerse.quote: "All our enemies open their mouths against us; panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction; my eyes flow with rivers of tears because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"All our enemies open their mouths against us;

panic and pitfall have come upon us, devastation and destruction;

Enemies jeer. And the calamity is described in pairs that pile on each other: panic and pitfall, devastation and destruction. Terror on the inside, traps on the outside, ruin all around.

my eyes flow with rivers of tears because of the destruction of the daughter of my people.

The we becomes my again. The speaker returns to his own tears — not a trickle but rivers. He is weeping not for himself now but for the daughter of my people. Personal pain has become grief for others.

That is a mark of maturity in suffering. Pain can shrink us so that we can see nothing but ourselves. Or it can enlarge us so that we weep with those who weep. Jesus, riding into the city where he would die, wept over it (Luke 19:41).

verseByVerse.quote: "My eyes will flow without ceasing, without respite, until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees; my eyes cause me grief at the fate of all the daughters of my city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"My eyes will flow without ceasing, without respite,

until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees;

Here is the goal of the tears: until the LORD from heaven looks down and sees. He will not stop weeping, and he will not stop praying, until God looks.

This is persistent prayer. Isaiah prayed the same: Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation (Isa 63:15). Jesus told a parable to the effect that they ought always to pray and not lose heart (Luke 18:1). There are prayers that need to be prayed many times, for many years, until the Lord looks down. Do not stop praying them.

my eyes cause me grief at the fate of all the daughters of my city.

What he sees makes him weep. He has watched the young women of Jerusalem suffer (1:4, 18; 2:21), and the memory of their faces does not leave him. Grief for others is not weakness. It is a heart like God's.

verseByVerse.quote: "I have been hunted like a bird by those who were my enemies without cause; they flung me alive into the pit and cast stones on me; water closed over my head; I said, 'I am lost.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I have been hunted like a bird by those who were my enemies without cause;

Now he tells a story of his own. He was hunted like a bird — small, defenceless, chased by people with nets. And they were his enemies without cause. He had done them no wrong.

That phrase echoes through the psalms: without cause they dug a pit for my life (Ps 35:7). Jesus took it up for himself: They hated me without a cause (John 15:25). The righteous sufferer who is hated for no reason finds his fullest meaning in Christ.

they flung me alive into the pit and cast stones on me;

Thrown into a pit alive, with stones thrown down on top. The ESV notes that the line may be rendered "they end my life in the pit" — they meant him to die there.

It is hard not to think of Jeremiah, whose enemies cast him into the cistern where there was no water in the cistern, but only mud, and Jeremiah sank in the mud (Jer 38:6), expecting him to die there of hunger (Jer 38:9).

water closed over my head; I said, 'I am lost.'

And now the water rises over his head. I am lost. Jonah said something very like it: The waters closed in over me to take my life (Jonah 2:5).

Many believers have been here — the moment when you say "This is the end; there is no way out." The next verse shows that it is not where the story ends.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 55–66 — You Came Near When I Called
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: From the bottom of the pit he called on the LORD's name, and the LORD heard: You came near when I called on you; you said, 'Do not fear!' (vv. 55-57). You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life (v. 58). So he asks God to judge his cause, since God has seen and heard every plot and taunt against him (vv. 59-63), and he ends by committing his enemies to the LORD's justice (vv. 64-66).
verseByVerse.theology: The God who seemed to shut out prayer is the God who comes near, speaks peace and redeems.

verseByVerse.quote: "I called on your name, O LORD, from the depths of the pit; you heard my plea, 'Do not close your ear to my cry for help!' You came near when I called on you; you said, 'Do not fear!'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I called on your name, O LORD, from the depths of the pit;

From the very bottom — the depths of the pit — he called on the LORD. No one can fall so far that he is out of calling distance. Out of the depths I cry to you, O LORD! (Ps 130:1).

you heard my plea, 'Do not close your ear to my cry for help!'

Remember verse 8: though I call and cry for help, he shuts out my prayer. And verse 44: no prayer can pass through. Now: you heard my plea. What felt like a locked door was not locked forever. The same man who said God had shut out his prayer now testifies that God heard it.

That is a word for anyone who is praying through the silence. How it feels now is not the last word on whether God hears.

You came near when I called on you; you said, 'Do not fear!'

Read this line slowly. You came near. God, who had seemed like a bear and a lion and an archer, comes near. And he speaks just three words: Do not fear!

That is the word God speaks again and again to his frightened people: fear not, for I am with you (Isa 41:10). It is the word Jesus spoke on the stormy lake: Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid (Matt 14:27). And it is the word the risen Christ spoke to John, who fell at his feet as though dead: Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore (Rev 1:17-18). The God who comes near to the man in the pit came near to us in person, went down into the pit of death himself, and came back up.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life. You have seen the wrong done to me, O LORD; judge my cause. You have seen all their vengeance, all their plots against me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You have taken up my cause, O Lord; you have redeemed my life.

Two legal pictures. You have taken up my cause — God has become his advocate in court. You have redeemed my life — God has paid to set him free, like a family member buying back a relative sold into slavery.

Jeremiah had promised exactly this for the exiles: Their Redeemer is strong; the LORD of hosts is his name. He will surely plead their cause (Jer 50:34).

And the New Testament shows how far this goes. If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). Our advocate does not only plead our case; he paid our debt. He is both the lawyer and the ransom.

You have seen the wrong done to me, O LORD; judge my cause.

You have seen all their vengeance, all their plots against me.

Twice: You have seen. The prayer of chapter 1 was Look, O LORD, and see. Now he knows God has seen. Every wrong, every plot. Nothing done in secret against God's people is hidden from him.

So he asks God to judge my cause. He does not take justice into his own hands. He hands his case to the one Judge who sees everything.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard their taunts, O LORD, all their plots against me. The lips and thoughts of my assailants are against me all the day long. Behold their sitting and their rising; I am the object of their taunts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You have heard their taunts, O LORD, all their plots against me.

The lips and thoughts of my assailants are against me all the day long.

Seen (vv. 59-60), and now heard. God hears what the enemies say out loud and knows what they only think — lips and thoughts. There is no private conversation hidden from him.

Behold their sitting and their rising; I am the object of their taunts.

Their sitting and their rising means everything they do from morning to night. Whether they sit down or get up, they are mocking him. You know when I sit down and when I rise up (Ps 139:2) — the God who knows every movement of his own people also knows every movement of their enemies.

If you are being slandered, mocked or plotted against, this is where to take it. Not into a counter-campaign, but to the God who has seen, and heard, and knows.

verseByVerse.quote: "You will repay them, O LORD, according to the work of their hands. You will give them dullness of heart; your curse will be on them. You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under your heavens, O LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You will repay them, O LORD, according to the work of their hands.

You will give them dullness of heart; your curse will be on them.

You will pursue them in anger and destroy them from under your heavens, O LORD."

The ESV notes that each of these lines can be read as a prayer rather than a statement: "Repay them," "Give them," "Pursue them" — and "place your curse" for your curse will be on them. The man is either declaring what God will do or asking him to do it. Either way he is leaving it with God.

And what he asks is simply justice: according to the work of their hands. Not more than they deserve. The Bible never tells believers to pretend that evil does not matter. God himself considers it just to repay with affliction those who afflict you (2 Thess 1:6).

Dullness of heart is a heart that can no longer take in the truth. It is a judgment God pronounced through Isaiah on a people who would not listen: Make the heart of this people dull, and their ears heavy, and blind their eyes (Isa 6:10). There is something more fearful than pain: a heart that no longer hears God. It is also a reason to pray, while the heart can still hear, for those who have not yet turned.

And listen to You will pursue them in anger. Earlier the people had said to God, You have wrapped yourself with anger and pursued us (v. 43). The prayer asks God to do to Babylon what he has done to Judah, as Zion had asked in the first poem (1:22). God's justice has no favourites. If his own people did not escape it, their oppressors will not either.

But notice where the vengeance is placed: in God's hands, not the man's. That is exactly the New Testament command: never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God (Rom 12:19). A believer who has truly handed justice over to God is free — free from bitterness, free to forgive, even free to pray for his enemies, as Jesus did on the cross (Luke 23:34). For the enemy who repents, Christ has already borne the curse (Gal 3:13).

The chapter's last words are from under your heavens, O LORD. The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "the heavens of the LORD." The chapter that began in darkness without any light ends looking up at the heavens that belong to the LORD — the same heavens from which, in verse 50, he waited for God to look down. He has not yet seen the end. But he has seen God come near, and that is enough to wait on.

3.title: His Mercies Are New Every Morning
3.overview:
Lamentations 3 is the heart of the book. One man now speaks, and he describes God as his attacker: he has been driven into darkness, broken, walled in, chained, hunted by a bear and a lion, used as a target for arrows, mocked by his own people and fed with wormwood and gravel. His prayer seems shut out, and at last he says his endurance has perished and his hope from the LORD is gone (vv. 1-18).

Then he calls something else to mind. The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is his faithfulness. The LORD is his portion, and so he will hope in him (vv. 19-24).

From there he teaches what he has learned. It is good to wait quietly for the LORD's salvation and to bear the yoke; to sit in silence, humble oneself and not strike back. The Lord will not cast off forever, and he does not afflict from his heart. He does not approve of injustice, yet nothing happens that he has not commanded, and no living man should complain about the punishment of his sins (vv. 25-39).

The I becomes we. The people are called to examine their ways, return to the LORD and confess their rebellion. God has wrapped himself in anger and in a cloud that blocks prayer, and they have become refuse among the nations. The speaker weeps until the LORD looks down, and recalls being hunted, thrown into a pit and overwhelmed by water (vv. 40-54). But he called on the LORD from the depths, and the LORD came near and said, Do not fear. God has taken up his cause and redeemed his life, and the man leaves his enemies to God's justice (vv. 55-66).

In Hebrew the chapter is an alphabetic poem in sets of three: sixty-six verses, three for each letter of the alphabet.
3.theology:
A believer may sink to the point of saying his hope is gone, and still be speaking to the LORD (v. 18). Hope returns not from changed circumstances but from calling to mind the character of God (v. 21).

The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases, and his mercies are new every morning; his faithfulness is great even among the ashes (vv. 22-23; Exod 34:6; 2 Tim 2:13). When every earthly portion is lost, the LORD himself remains the portion of his people (v. 24; Num 18:20; Ps 73:26).

Affliction is ordained by God, yet it does not come from his heart; compassion according to his abundant steadfast love always follows grief for his people (vv. 31-33; Ezek 33:11; Heb 12:10).

God is sovereign over good and bad alike, yet he never approves of human injustice; the instruments of his judgment remain guilty (vv. 34-38; Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23).

Lament is right; complaint against God's justice is not (v. 39). True repentance examines its own ways, lifts up the heart as well as the hands, and confesses without excuse (vv. 40-42).

God hears prayer from the depths, comes near, and says Do not fear; he is his people's advocate and redeemer (vv. 55-58; Jer 50:34). In Christ the barrier to prayer is torn away, and the believer has an advocate who also paid the ransom (Matt 27:51; Heb 7:25; 1 John 2:1).

Justice against enemies belongs to God, and leaving it with him sets the believer free to forgive (vv. 64-66; Rom 12:19; Luke 23:34).

The man of affliction, mocked, struck on the cheek, hated without cause and thrown into the pit, points beyond himself to Christ, who suffered all this not for his own sins but for ours (vv. 14, 30, 52-53; Isa 50:6; John 15:25; 1 Pet 2:23).
3.examples:
Darkness without any light.

A prayer that feels like it hits the ceiling.

Bread full of gravel.

A man who has forgotten what good is.

Replaying the same pain night after night.

But this I call to mind — taking hold of a railing in the dark.

Manna gathered morning by morning; mercy that cannot be stored up.

Losing the land and discovering that your portion is the LORD.

A young ox learning to pull.

A mouth in the dust, and a door left open: there may yet be hope.

A Father who corrects with a heavy heart.

The curtain torn from top to bottom.

A man at the bottom of a cistern, calling.

You came near; you said, Do not fear.
